topics.title: Present tense: person endings and the irregular verbs
topics.summary: Italian usually drops the subject pronoun, so the verb ending alone says who is acting. Each of the six persons has its own ending in the presente, and about twenty very common verbs have irregular forms. The idea that makes it click: find the real subject first (a pronoun you cannot see, or a noun phrase), turn it into io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi or loro, then pick that one form.

topics.title: c'è and ci sono against è and sono; avere and fare where English has to be
topics.summary: English uses to be for almost everything; Italian splits the job. C'è / ci sono say that something exists or is present, è / sono say what or where a known thing is, stare covers health, avere covers hunger, cold and age, fare covers the weather. The idea that makes it click: ask whether you are introducing something new (c'è) or describing something already known (è).

topics.title: Adjective agreement: gender and number endings
topics.summary: An Italian adjective copies the gender and number of the noun it describes, after the noun and after essere alike: la casa è nuova, le case sono nuove. The idea that makes it click: do not rhyme with the noun. Ask what gender and number the noun is, then pick the ending from the adjective's own set: -o / -a / -i / -e, or -e / -i.
